# Baselines and the fair-comparison protocol {#sec-baselines}

Every accuracy claim in this book compares MeshTransformer2 (MT2) against
GeoTransolver, and where stated against plain Transolver, under one protocol
that fixes everything except the architecture: matched sampled points per
case and epochs, each architecture at its own best learning rate, two or
more seeds, shared validation cases, and sealed test splits opened once. The
baselines are strong, not straw: GeoTransolver has at least as many
parameters as MT2 (9.0M against 8.9M), trains in more memory (4.6 GB against
3.6 GB at 10,000 tokens), and receives raw coordinates that MT2 never sees.
Two questions are settled here so that the results chapters need not carry
them: MT2's exact equivariance is *not* an accuracy advantage over a
canonicalized GeoTransolver (exactly pose-invariant at 1.01x cost), and
learning-rate choice belongs to the protocol because a shared rate would
have decided the comparison by tuning.

## The baselines and what each one sees

**The comparison is against two members of the Transolver family: the same
soft-slice attention as MT2, fed raw geometric inputs in place of MT2's
invariants.** Transolver (Wu et al., ICML 2024, arXiv
[2402.02366](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02366)) is a transformer for physics
fields on unstructured point sets. Each layer assigns every point a softmax
mixture over a fixed number of *slices*, pools point features into one token
per slice, runs attention among the slice tokens, and scatters the result
back through the same mixture. MT2 (@sec-mt2) shares this backbone; it
differs in what enters the routing and what the tokens may carry.

**GeoTransolver** is the recipe's reference surface model. Per surface point
it receives the coordinates (centered on the case) and the unit normal as a
six-channel feature; the freestream velocity vector is a three-channel global
feature. Its *geometry encoder* takes the coordinates a second time through a
dedicated embedding path that conditions the slice attention; the ball-query
local-feature path (`include_local_features`) is off throughout this program.
Twelve layers, hidden width 256, 256 slices, 9.0M parameters. It is not
rotation- or translation-equivariant: rotate the car and it sees a different
input.

**Transolver** is the same family without the geometry encoder, the control
that isolates what the encoder contributes. Per point it receives coordinates
and normal; the freestream vector is broadcast to every point. Eight layers,
hidden 256, 256 slices, 6.0M parameters. On the recipe datasets it trains at
learning rate 3e-3, its best of the two rates run, where GeoTransolver and
MT2 use 1e-3.

**MT2** receives position, unit normal and cell area per point and the unit
freestream direction as its only global input, consumed through invariants
and equivariant anchors only (@sec-mt2): 12 layers, hidden 192, 256 slices,
8.9M parameters.

| architecture | per-point inputs | global input | layers | hidden | slices | parameters | peak memory at 10k tokens |
|---|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| MeshTransformer2 | position, unit normal, cell area (via invariants and anchors only) | unit freestream direction | 12 | 192 | 256 | 8.9M | 3.6 GB |
| GeoTransolver | centered coordinates, unit normal; coordinates again through the geometry encoder | freestream velocity vector | 12 | 256 | 256 | 9.0M | 4.6 GB |
| Transolver | centered coordinates, unit normal | freestream velocity vector, broadcast per point | 8 | 256 | 256 | 6.0M | not measured |

: The three architectures compared on the aerodynamic datasets. *Per-point
inputs*: channels attached to each of the 10,000 sampled surface points per
case. *Global input*: the one per-case vector. *Layers*: soft-slice attention
blocks in the encoder. *Hidden*: width of the per-point feature vector.
*Slices*: slice tokens per layer. *Parameters*: trainable parameters of the
recipe configuration. *Peak memory*: largest allocated GPU memory over one
forward-plus-backward step on one case of 10,000 sampled points in bfloat16
(GeoTransolver's figure is from its training run, which adds under 0.2 GB of
optimizer state); not measured for Transolver, which serves only as a
same-family control on HiLiftAeroML. Configuration source:
`unified_external_aero_recipe/conf/model/{mt2,geotransolver,transolver}_surface.yaml`.
{#tbl-architectures}

## Transolver on the controlled suites {#sec-part-baseline}

**On the synthetic boundary-to-interior suites (@sec-linear-suites) the
mainstream baseline is a steel-manned Transolver, and the exact-kernel
MeshTransformer (MT1, @sec-mt1) beats it by 7.7–20x at matched parameters
where exact operator structure applies, narrowing to 1.4x where MT1 is itself
representation-limited.** The comparison ablates the thesis of the controlled
suites; it does not rank architectures for industrial use.

### The matched-capacity comparison {#sec-transolver}

The baseline is a port of Transolver verified against the official
implementation, given a *shared boundary-plus-query token sequence* (its
query points attend to each other and to the boundary, more interaction than
MT1, whose queries are independent by contract), and trained exactly as MT1:
streaming generation of one fresh case per step, AdamW at 3e-4, seeds
17/29/43. Two capacities: *matched*, 103,053 parameters against MT1's
104,261, and *native*, 2,809,409 (27x).

The quantity is relative L2 error of the interior field on the frozen 2D
Laplace reference banks, in-distribution (ID) and on a held-out band of
boundary-condition frequencies (frequency-OOD); similarity covariance is the
relative change of the prediction under a random rotation, translation and
rescaling. At matched parameters and 3,000 steps Transolver reaches ID 0.769
against MT1's 0.0375. At native capacity its step curve descends 0.608,
0.262, 0.119 over 3k, 10k, 30k steps: with 27x the parameters and 10x the
compute it stays 3.2x above MT1. Frequency-OOD saturates near 0.46 against
0.0748; similarity covariance stays at 0.08–0.25 at every budget against
MT1's 3e-7. On Transolver's own fixed-dataset regime the matched-parameter
gap is 7.7x; on the screened and 3D suites 34–78x; 1.4x on the
multiply-connected shell suite, where MT1 is itself representation-limited.
Transolver keeps
what this benchmark does not test: volumetric and piecewise inputs, which
boundary-only MT1 cannot ingest. Data: `results/learned_bie_2026-07-02.json`,
keys `iteration_15_transolver_comparison`, `iteration_17_fixed_dataset_regime`.

## The fair-comparison protocol {#sec-fair-comparison}

**Every cross-architecture number in this book was produced under the
following protocol; a comparison that violates any item is not reported.**
Datasets and splits are defined in @sec-problem, the metric in @sec-metrics.

1. **Matched tokens per case: 10,000 sampled surface points for every
   architecture.** Accuracy still rises with tokens at 10,000 (6,500 to
   10,000 is worth 8% for MT2, @sec-resource-matching), so a token mismatch
   would be a handicap disguised as an architecture difference.
2. **Matched epochs: 500 for every arm, one case per step.** A short budget
   favours the faster starter; the 1,000-epoch GeoTransolver controls at 35
   and 210 training cases (@sec-data-efficiency) check that 500 does not
   under-train the baseline.
3. **Learning rate chosen per architecture on the full split, by
   validation, before any ladder or ablation ran.** From the grid
   {1e-3, 3e-3, 1e-2}: 1e-3 for MT2 and GeoTransolver, 3e-3 for Transolver,
   then frozen for every smaller split and ablation. Choosing after seeing
   ladder results would let the tuning budget set the gap (@sec-lr-protocol).
4. **Two or more seeds per cell, reported individually.** Seed spread is
   the only noise estimate at 48 or 180 validation cases; every ratio is
   quoted with both seeds so the reader can see whether it exceeds the
   spread.
5. **Shared validation cases.** All architectures are scored on the same
   180 HiLiftAeroML cases or 48 DrivAerML cars, sampled with the same seed.
6. **Paired per-case statistics where a ratio is claimed.** A ratio of
   means can be carried by a few cases, so the count of validation cases on
   which one architecture is more accurate, with median and worst-decile
   per-case ratios, is reported alongside (@sec-data-efficiency).
7. **Sealed test splits evaluated once.** The 360-case HiLiftAeroML test
   set and the regime-extrapolation test lists (@sec-regime-extrapolation)
   are taken verbatim from the dataset manifest and evaluated a single time.
8. **Preregistered bars.** Each experiment states, in readout units and
   before it runs, the value that confirms and the value that refutes.

### One instrument per dataset {#sec-review-instrument}

The *instrument* for a dataset is its fixed validation set and evaluation
configuration: on DrivAerML, surface pressure and wall shear on 48 held-out
cars at 10,000 sampled cells; on HiLiftAeroML, pressure, velocity, wall
shear, temperature and density on 180 held-out cases shared by every training
split. An instrument is never widened after a result is read from it; a
control that changes it (another token count, a rotated pose, a biased
sampling density) is reported as such, never mixed into an in-family number.
Its limits bind where stated: 48 cars is a small validation set and two seeds
a thin noise estimate (@sec-limits).

## Resource matching {#sec-resource-matching}

**At the recipe operating point MT2 uses no more parameters and less memory
than GeoTransolver, so no MT2 accuracy figure is bought with resources.**
Parameters 8.9M against 9.0M; tokens per case 10,000 each; peak training
memory at 10,000 tokens 3.6 GB against 4.6 GB, with MT2 at 283 ms per
forward-plus-backward step on an RTX 4090 in bfloat16.

One accounting note. MT2's relational read-back pools eight scalar
point–anchor invariants over slices and projects them to the hidden width.
Two implementations compute the same function: projecting each point–slice
pair and then pooling stores a points x slices x hidden/2 tensor per layer
for the backward pass, about 0.5 GB per layer, and peaks at 9.8 GB; pooling
first and then projecting is the same affine map moved through the softmax
mixture, stores points x 8 per layer, and peaks at 3.6 GB. With identical
weights the two agree to 4e-15 maximum absolute difference in fp64. The
trained MT2 checkpoints in this book came from the 9.8 GB implementation, but
since it evaluates the same function with the same parameters, no reported
accuracy depended on the extra memory (@sec-nb-geo-pool-memory).

The direct test of whether memory buys MT2 accuracy is to take memory away.
@tbl-matched-memory reports DrivAerML validation pressure error, relative L2
per car averaged over 48 cars, at the frozen rate 3e-3 for both architectures
(not MT2's best rate; the comparison of interest is MT2 against MT2). Cutting
MT2's tokens from 10,000 to 6,500 brings its peak memory in the pairwise
implementation to 6.56 GB, 33% less, and costs 8% accuracy. That is a token
effect, not a memory effect: the same 10,000-token model fits in 3.6 GB.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-matched-memory
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
import json
from pathlib import Path

R = Path("..") / "results"
iw = json.load(open(R / "instrument_wave_reduction_2026-09-01.json"))
p = lambda k: iw[k]["pressure_l2"]
mt2_10k = [p(f"ref_mt2_v3c_seed{s}") for s in (42, 43)]
mt2_65 = [p(f"iw_mt2_v3c_r6500_seed{s}") for s in (42, 43)]
gt_10k = [p(f"ref_gt_fixed_seed{s}") for s in (42, 43)]
mean = lambda v: sum(v) / len(v)
ratio = mean(mt2_65) / mean(mt2_10k)
rows = [
    ("MeshTransformer2", "10,000", "3.6 GB (9.8 GB pairwise implementation)", mt2_10k, 1.0),
    ("MeshTransformer2", "6,500", "6.56 GB (pairwise implementation)", mt2_65, ratio),
    ("GeoTransolver", "10,000", "4.6 GB", gt_10k, None),
]
out = "| architecture | tokens per case | peak training memory | pressure rel-L2 (seed 42 / 43) | relative to MT2 at 10,000 |\n|---|--:|---|---|--:|\n"
for n, t, m, v, r in rows:
    rr = "--" if r is None else f"{r:.2f}x"
    out += f"| {n} | {t} | {m} | {v[0]:.4f} / {v[1]:.4f} | {rr} |\n"
print(out)
print(": The matched-memory control on DrivAerML. *Tokens per case*: sampled "
      "surface cells per car in training and validation. *Peak training "
      "memory*: as defined for @tbl-architectures; the 6,500-token row was "
      "measured with the pairwise implementation, which produced these "
      "checkpoints. *Pressure rel-L2*: relative L2 error of surface pressure "
      "per car, mean over the 48 validation cars, at learning rate 3e-3 for "
      "every row (not MT2's best rate). The last column divides the row's "
      "seed mean by that of MT2 at 10,000 tokens. Not shown: wall shear, "
      "which moves the same way. Data: "
      "results/instrument_wave_reduction_2026-09-01.json.")
print("{#tbl-matched-memory}")
```

## Pose: equivariant by construction, invariant by canonicalization {#sec-pose}

**MT2 is exactly rotation- and translation-covariant by construction;
GeoTransolver trained in a canonical frame is exactly pose-invariant at 1.01x
accuracy cost. On vehicle data the two are equally good, so equivariance is a
contract about what the model needs at inference, not an accuracy
advantage.**

The two phrases mean different things. A model is *equivariant by
construction* when every operation inside it commutes with rigid motions: its
inputs are invariants or vectors in an equivariant basis, so a rotated case
yields the rotated prediction to floating-point roundoff (MT2's fp64 contract
test, @sec-mt2). A pipeline is *invariant by canonicalization* when a
preprocessing step estimates a frame from each case, expresses the case in
that frame, runs an ordinary non-equivariant model, and rotates vector outputs
back; it is invariant exactly when the frame estimate depends on the
pose-free geometry alone.

The canonical frame used here sends the freestream direction to +x and fixes
the roll about it from the area-weighted principal axes of the surface in the
transverse plane, sign from the third moment. On DrivAerML no case is within
5% of a principal-axis degeneracy and the sign is consistent across all 48
validation cars. Estimated from the 10,000 sampled cells the model sees, the
frame is tilted 0.8° on average from the full-resolution frame
(@sec-nb-p1-canon-verdict).

@tbl-pose reports DrivAerML validation pressure error, relative L2 per car
averaged over 48 cars, for GeoTransolver at learning rate 3e-3, 500 epochs,
two seeds, evaluated *in pose* (cars as the dataset provides them) and on an
*SO(3) orbit* (each car in a uniformly random orientation, rotation angles
44–179°), vector outputs rotated back before scoring.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-pose
#| output: asis
#| code-fold: true
import json
from pathlib import Path

R = Path("..") / "results"
p1 = json.load(open(R / "p1_canonicalization_control_2026-09-02.json"))
pp = json.load(open(R / "p1pp_canonical_training_2026-09-03.json"))
raw_in = [p1["table"][f"inpose|raw|gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]
raw_orb = [p1["table"][f"orbit|raw|gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]
eval_canon_in = [p1["table"][f"inpose|canon|gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]
eval_canon_orb = [p1["table"][f"orbit|canon|gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in (42, 43)]
tr_in = [pp["results"][f"gt_canon_seed{s}"]["inpose_canon"][0] for s in (42, 43)]
tr_orb = [pp["results"][f"gt_canon_seed{s}"]["orbit_SO3_canon"][0] for s in (42, 43)]
mean = lambda v: sum(v) / len(v)
ref = mean(raw_in)
orbit_ratios = [v / p1["prior"]["gt_inpose_pressure_l2"]
                for v in p1["prior"]["gt_p1_orbit_pressure_l2"].values()]
fx = lambda r: f"{r:.0f}x" if r >= 10 else f"{r:.2f}x"
def row(name, a, b):
    return (f"| {name} | {a[0]:.4f} / {a[1]:.4f} ({fx(mean(a)/ref)}) "
            f"| {b[0]:.4f} / {b[1]:.4f} ({fx(mean(b)/ref)}) |\n")
out = "| GeoTransolver variant | in pose (seed 42 / 43) | SO(3) orbit (seed 42 / 43) |\n|---|---|---|\n"
out += row("trained and evaluated in the recipe frame", raw_in, raw_orb)
out += row("trained in the recipe frame, canonicalized at inference only", eval_canon_in, eval_canon_orb)
out += row("trained and evaluated in the canonical frame", tr_in, tr_orb)
print(out)
print(f": Pose dependence of GeoTransolver on DrivAerML. *In pose*: the 48 "
      f"validation cars in the orientation the dataset provides. *SO(3) "
      f"orbit*: the same cars, each in a uniformly random orientation. Cells "
      f"are surface-pressure relative L2 averaged over the 48 cars, seed 42 / "
      f"seed 43; the parenthesized factor divides the seed mean by the "
      f"in-pose seed mean of the first row ({ref:.4f}). Across three seeds "
      f"of the recipe-frame model the orbit penalty spans "
      f"{min(orbit_ratios):.0f}–{max(orbit_ratios):.0f}x. Not shown: MT2, "
      f"whose orbit and in-pose predictions agree to fp64 roundoff by "
      f"construction; wall shear behaves the same way. Data: "
      f"results/p1_canonicalization_control_2026-09-02.json (rows 1–2), "
      f"results/p1pp_canonical_training_2026-09-03.json (row 3).")
print("{#tbl-pose}")
```

Three things follow. First, GeoTransolver in the recipe frame is not
pose-robust: a random orientation takes it to 26–32x its in-pose error,
worse than predicting the freestream pressure everywhere. Second,
canonicalization must be in the training pipeline. Applied only at inference
to a model trained in one exact pose it is pose-invariant but costs 1.6–1.7x,
because that model is hypersensitive to sub-degree frame tilt (a fixed 1°
roll costs it 1.7x, 5° costs 6.5x) and the frame estimate carries about 0.8°
of it; a model that sees the estimator's tilt noise during training learns to
ignore it, and the penalty falls to 1.01x (@sec-nb-p1pp-verdict). Third, on
this data MT2's exact equivariance and canonicalized GeoTransolver deliver
the same pose invariance, so no accuracy claim in this book is attributed to
equivariance; the pose contract is scored as a contract.

What the contract still buys is generality. Canonicalization needs a known
freestream direction at inference and a principal frame whose sign can be
resolved; both hold for every vehicle and wing dataset here. They fail for a
PDE surrogate with no distinguished drive direction, for bodies whose
transverse inertia tensor is degenerate or whose third moment vanishes (a
symmetry the estimator cannot break), and for assemblies of parts in mixed
orientations, where no single frame canonicalizes every component. MT2 needs
neither a frame estimate nor a freestream at inference; there the contract
is the difference between a working surrogate and a 26–32x failure.

## Learning-rate sensitivity is part of the protocol {#sec-lr-protocol}

**The two architectures differ by an order of magnitude in how much accuracy
they lose at a wrong learning rate, so a protocol sharing one rate would
measure tuning luck instead of architecture.** @fig-lr reports validation
pressure error, relative L2 per case averaged over the validation cases, at
500 epochs and 10,000 tokens, for every rate run on the full splits: on
DrivAerML (435 training cars, 48 validation) the grid {1e-3, 3e-3, 1e-2},
two seeds per rung; on HiLiftAeroML (1,260 training cases, 180 validation)
the grid {1e-3, 3e-3}, two seeds per rung.

```{python}
#| label: fig-lr
#| fig-cap: >
#|   Learning-rate sensitivity on the full splits. Validation pressure
#|   relative L2 (mean over the 48 DrivAerML cars, left, or the 180
#|   HiLiftAeroML cases, right) against learning rate, log–log, for
#|   GeoTransolver (red circles) and MeshTransformer2 (blue squares). Large
#|   markers joined by lines are two-seed means; small markers are the
#|   individual seeds; the y axis is shared. Not shown: Transolver, run only
#|   at the two smaller rates on the sub-splits; wall shear and the other
#|   fields, which order the same way.
#|   Data: results/instrument_wave_reduction_2026-09-01.json (DrivAerML)
#|   and results/highlift_wave_reduction.json (HiLiftAeroML).
#| code-fold: true
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib as mpl
# book palette (mirrors figures.py without importing it: that module
# switches matplotlib to Agg, which suppresses inline output here)
BLUE, RED, GREY = "#2a78d6", "#e34948", "#52514e"
INK, INK2, MUTED, GRID, BASELINE = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#e1e0d9", "#c3c2b7"
mpl.rcParams.update({"figure.dpi": 110, "font.size": 10, "axes.edgecolor": BASELINE,
                     "axes.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID,
                     "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED, "xtick.labelcolor": INK2,
                     "ytick.labelcolor": INK2, "axes.spines.top": False,
                     "axes.spines.right": False, "legend.frameon": False})

R = Path("..") / "results"
iw = json.load(open(R / "instrument_wave_reduction_2026-09-01.json"))
hl = json.load(open(R / "highlift_wave_reduction.json"))
S = (42, 43)
drivaer = {
    "GeoTransolver": {1e-3: [iw[f"iw_gt_lr1e3_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in S],
                      3e-3: [iw[f"ref_gt_fixed_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in S],
                      1e-2: [iw[f"iw_gt_lr1e2_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in S]},
    "MeshTransformer2": {1e-3: [iw[f"iw_mt2_lr1e3_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in S],
                         3e-3: [iw[f"ref_mt2_v3c_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in S],
                         1e-2: [iw[f"iw_mt2_lr1e2_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in S]},
}
hilift = {
    "GeoTransolver": {1e-3: [hl[f"gt_hl_lr1_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in S],
                      3e-3: [hl[f"gt_hl_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in S]},
    "MeshTransformer2": {1e-3: [hl[f"mt2_hl_lr1_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in S],
                         3e-3: [hl[f"mt2_hl_seed{s}"]["pressure_l2"] for s in S]},
}
style = {"GeoTransolver": (RED, "o"), "MeshTransformer2": (BLUE, "s")}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.2, 3.9), sharey=True)
panels = ((drivaer, "DrivAerML, 435 training cars", (7e-4, 2.6e-2), (1e-3, 3e-3, 1e-2)),
          (hilift, "HiLiftAeroML, 1,260 training cases", (7e-4, 6e-3), (1e-3, 3e-3)))
for ax, (data, title, xlim, ticks) in zip(axes, panels):
    for name, series in data.items():
        color, marker = style[name]
        lrs = sorted(series)
        means = [statistics.mean(series[lr]) for lr in lrs]
        ax.plot(lrs, means, "-", color=color, lw=1.6, marker=marker, ms=7,
                mec="white", mew=1.0, zorder=3)
        for lr in lrs:
            for v in series[lr]:
                ax.plot(lr, v, marker, color=color, ms=3.5, alpha=0.75, zorder=4)
        ax.annotate(name, (lrs[-1], means[-1]), xytext=(7, 0),
                    textcoords="offset points", color=color, va="center",
                    fontsize=9, fontweight="bold")
    ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set_xlim(*xlim); ax.set_ylim(0.03, 1.0)
    ax.set_xticks(ticks); ax.set_xticklabels([f"{t:g}" for t in ticks])
    ax.minorticks_off()
    ax.set_xlabel("learning rate [–] (log)")
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10, color=INK2, loc="left")
axes[0].set_ylabel("validation pressure rel-L2 [–] (log)")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

On DrivAerML, GeoTransolver's best rate is 3e-3 (0.0532) and at 1e-2 it
degrades 4–14x (0.221 and 0.739 on the two seeds); MT2's best is 1e-3
(0.0577) and at 1e-2 it degrades 1.55x. On HiLiftAeroML both are best at
1e-3, where they are at parity (@sec-full-data); at 3e-3 GeoTransolver
destabilizes to 0.148 and 0.397, while MT2's eight lane results across both
rates and both seeds span 0.040–0.049 (@sec-nb-hl-verdict). The robustness is reported as a
result in @sec-robustness-lr; here the point is procedural.

Two consequences are built into the protocol. First, because GeoTransolver's
best rate differs between datasets (3e-3 on DrivAerML, 1e-3 on HiLiftAeroML),
"best rate per architecture, chosen on the full split" is the only rule under
which the GeoTransolver baseline is the strongest version of itself on both.
The DrivAerML best-vs-best figure is MT2 0.0577 against GeoTransolver 0.0532,
MT2 1.085x behind; at GeoTransolver's rate it would read 1.19x, at MT2's rate
1.05x (@sec-full-data). Second, the rate is chosen once and frozen for every
smaller split: retuning at 35 or 210 training cases would hand the baseline
search that MT2 did not get, and the steel-man controls in
@sec-data-efficiency (GeoTransolver at 3e-3 and at 1,000 epochs on the small
splits) confirm that the frozen rate does not produce the data-efficiency
gap.
